say.text: A 40-year-old man has hereditary spherocytosis, chronic haemolysis and gallstones. Which stone is he most likely to have, and where does it form?

choices.label: Brown pigment stones, formed in the bile ducts
Black pigment stones, formed in the bile ducts
Black pigment stones, formed in the gallbladder
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with the cause the stem gives you: red cells breaking down early. Which stone goes with that, and where does it form?
Yes. Chronic haemolysis is the clue: black stones are small, multiple and hard, form in the gallbladder, and go with cirrhosis.
That choice is not right.
Brown stones are soft and earthy and go with infected bile and stasis, not with haemolysis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair the cause with the stone: haemolysis does not point to the soft, infected-bile stone.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The colour is right but the site is not: black stones form in the gallbladder, while duct stones in infected bile are the soft, earthy type.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so split the site from the colour: duct stones in infection are soft and earthy.

say.text: Step one: the cause in the stem is chronic haemolysis. Step two: the stone that goes with it is black, formed in the gallbladder.
Step three: black stones are small, multiple and hard, and also go with cirrhosis.
Black pigment stones are small, multiple and hard, form in the gallbladder, and go with haemolysis and cirrhosis.
Brown pigment stones are soft and earthy, form in infected bile in the ducts, and bacterial enzymes help make them.

choices.label: Brown pigment stones, formed in the gallbladder
Brown pigment stones, formed in the bile ducts
Black pigment stones, formed in the gallbladder
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the cause the stem gives you: a parasite and repeated infection. Which pigment is tied to infection, not to haemolysis?
That choice is not right.
The pigment is right but the site is not: brown stones need bacterial enzymes in infected bile, and that bile sits in the ducts.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the site separately from the pigment: infected bile stagnates in the ducts.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Black stones go with haemolysis and cirrhosis, while this stem gives a worm and repeated cholangitis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair each pigment with its cause: black with haemolysis, not with worms and cholangitis.

say.text: Yes. Brown pigment stones are soft and earthy, form in the bile ducts, and go with infection and stasis.
The worm and the cholangitis are the infection link, and bacterial enzymes in infected bile favour this stone.
Cholesterol stones have their own risk factors. Think female, fat, fertile and forty, often with fair added.
Oestrogens and pregnancy raise biliary cholesterol, and obesity or rapid weight loss add to the risk.

choices.label: Oral contraceptive use, raising biliary cholesterol
Chronic haemolysis, as in hereditary spherocytosis
Biliary infection with Ascaris, in the ducts
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think of the female and hormone clues in the mnemonic, and of body fat and weight, not of the blood or of worms.
That choice is not right.
Chronic haemolysis is the cause tied to black pigment stones, not to cholesterol stones.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the haemolysis stone apart from the cholesterol risk factors.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Infection and parasites are the cause tied to brown pigment stones, while cholesterol stones follow hormones, fat and weight.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so match infection to brown stones, and the cholesterol risks to hormones and weight.

say.text: Yes. Oestrogens and oral contraceptives raise biliary cholesterol secretion, and progesterone slows the gallbladder, so they add to cholesterol stones.
Compare acute cholecystitis with a stone (calculous) and without one (acalculous). Which is true of the acalculous form?

choices.label: Runs a milder course, as no stone obstructs
Has lower mortality, as patients are younger
Has more gangrene, perforation and higher mortality
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the patient, not the stone. What happens to blood flow and bile flow in a critically ill patient?
That choice is not right.
This form starts from stasis and ischaemia in critically ill patients, so having no stone does not mean a milder course.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the mechanism: stasis and ischaemia drive this disease, not the stone.

say.text: That choice is not right.
This form strikes sick patients after burns, sepsis or major surgery, so youth is not what drives it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check who gets this disease: the critically ill.

say.text: The answer is worse. Acalculous disease comes from stasis and ischaemia in critically ill patients.
So it has more gangrene and perforation than calculous disease, and a higher mortality.
Yes. Acalculous disease comes from stasis and ischaemia in critically ill patients, so gangrene, perforation and mortality run higher.
A burns patient on day four in the intensive care unit (ICU) has fever and right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain. Ultrasound shows no stone. What should you plan around?

choices.label: Low risk, since no stone is present
Gangrene and perforation risk is high
It will settle with analgesia, as biliary colic does
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Set aside whether a stone is present. What does a critically ill patient's gallbladder suffer from, and what can that do to its wall?
That choice is not right.
Stasis and ischaemia in a burns patient can damage the wall with no stone at all.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember that a stone-free gallbladder can still be the sick one.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Biliary colic is a transient pain, while this is inflammation of the wall from ischaemia, and it runs a worse course.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep colic apart from cholecystitis: fever with RUQ pain means inflammation, not a passing spasm.

say.text: Yes. In a critically ill patient, stasis and ischaemia can gangrene or perforate the wall without any stone.
No stone means no obstruction, yet the wall still fails from stasis and ischaemia. This form is about 5 to 10 per cent of cases.
Its gangrene, perforation and mortality run higher than in calculous disease, so a stone-free label never means safe.
